item.title: Nvidia earnings could test a fragile market. Five stocks are already offering clues
item.description:
Nvidia earnings could test a fragile market. Five stocks are already offering clues.

investingLive's latest earnings-mood assessment stands at just 4 out of 10. Recent results show a market willing to reward some companies aggressively, but also quick to punish others and unwilling to sustain some of its initial enthusiasm. CoreWeave provides a particularly revealing example.

Nvidia (NVDA) reports quarterly earnings on Tuesday, November 17, and the AI chip leader faces an increasingly selective market.

According to investingLive's latest earnings-regime research, Wall Street's reaction to recent corporate results has turned mildly defensive, with an Earnings Mood reading of approximately 4 out of 10.

The concern is not simply whether companies are reporting strong financial results. It is how investors react to those results and, perhaps more importantly, whether the initial stock-price gains can survive the following trading sessions.

That distinction could become particularly important for Nvidia this week.

investingLive's Earnings Mood: 4/10, with caution replacing optimism

Latest assessment: November 13, 2026

Earnings Mood: 4/10

Classification: Cautious / mildly defensive

Recent direction: Cooling after a brief improvement

The reading suggests that the recent earnings environment is less supportive than neutral. It does not indicate panic, nor does it suggest that every earnings reporter is struggling.

Instead, the market is demonstrating a pattern of selective enthusiasm, substantial negative reactions and, in several notable cases, an inability to preserve positive post-earnings moves.

The assessment reflects observed market behavior and editorial judgment. It is not a calibrated probability of an upcoming decline or a trading signal.

What the last four earnings sessions reveal

The latest four completed U.S. earnings-reaction sessions show an interesting sequence.

Across the four sessions, investingLive's research covered 723 usable company earnings-reaction observations, of which approximately 43.3% were positive.

Three of the four sessions delivered negative capitalization-weighted results.

These figures describe the reactions of reporting companies, not the performance of the S&P 500 or Nasdaq indices.

November 11 provided a welcome improvement. More than 61% of the reporting-company reactions were positive, while the capitalization-weighted result reached +2.63%.

However, the improvement did not broaden into a sustained positive environment. The following two sessions returned to negative capitalization-weighted readings, with positive breadth falling below 43% on both days.

That is an important distinction for traders.

A single strong session can demonstrate that investors remain willing to buy. But a sustained improvement requires more than one successful day. Ideally, additional reporting companies should participate, influential stocks should contribute positively and the initial gains should hold.

So far, the recent evidence is mixed, with a defensive tilt.

Why Nvidia's earnings are an important test

Nvidia is not just another company reporting quarterly results.

It is a major force in AI infrastructure, a significant component of leading U.S. stock indices and an important reference point for investor expectations surrounding AI spending.

Its results can therefore influence sentiment well beyond its own share price, particularly across semiconductors, AI infrastructure providers and technology stocks.

Nvidia is scheduled to release results on Tuesday, November 17, after the U.S. market close, followed by its earnings conference call at 5:00 p.m. ET.

But investors should distinguish three separate questions:

Three questions for Nvidia investors1. Were Nvidia's results and guidance strong? Revenue, profitability, forward guidance and management commentary will help establish the fundamental picture. 2. How did the stock initially respond? A strong report does not automatically produce a positive share-price reaction if expectations were even higher. 3. Did investors continue supporting the reaction? Sustained gains, or a successful recovery after an initial setback, could provide more constructive evidence than a brief after-hours rally.

The third question is especially relevant in the current earnings environment.

To see why, consider what happened to CoreWeave last week.

CoreWeave: The earnings winner that gave back nearly two-thirds of its initial advance

CoreWeave (CRWV), the AI infrastructure company, delivered one of last week's most interesting post-earnings reactions.

Following its November 10 quarterly report, shares advanced sharply on November 11.

The initial response was impressive.

But the subsequent price behavior tells a more complicated story.

CoreWeave's post-earnings price sequence

CoreWeave (CRWV): November 10-13November 10: $48.73The regular-session close immediately before earnings.November 11: $60.77A gain of approximately 24.7% in the first post-earnings session.November 12: $56.60Shares surrendered some of their initial gains.November 13: $53.13The stock remained approximately 9.0% above its pre-earnings close.

By Friday, only approximately 36.5% of the original dollar advance remained.

That means nearly two-thirds of the initial gain had disappeared within two trading sessions.

Friday's price action adds another important clue

The closing prices alone do not tell the entire story.

On Friday, November 13, CoreWeave traded as low as $49.24, coming within just $0.51 of its pre-earnings closing price of $48.73.

Shares subsequently recovered to close at $53.13.

This creates two competing observations.

On the bearish side, the substantial retreat from $60.77 suggests that the market was not prepared to maintain the initial earnings enthusiasm.

On the more constructive side, buyers did push the stock away from Friday's intraday low, preventing an almost complete erasure of the initial earnings advance by the closing bell.

That recovery matters, although one intraday rebound does not establish a lasting reversal.

The next important question is whether CoreWeave begins repairing the damage or resumes surrendering its remaining earnings gains.

A recovery toward $60.77 would suggest renewed acceptance of the higher post-earnings valuation.

A sustained move toward, or below, the $48.73 pre-earnings reference would point to a more complete rejection of the original rally.

These are historical closing-price references, not guaranteed turning points.

For traders and investors, the broader lesson is simple:

A stock can still be up significantly after earnings while its underlying price response is deteriorating.

Watching only the initial earnings-day percentage gain can create a misleading impression of strength.

CoreWeave is our highest-priority independent post-earnings stock to monitor this week, even before Nvidia reports.

Four more stocks revealing what investors are rewarding and rejecting

CoreWeave is not an isolated example. Recent earnings reactions across several influential companies offer useful comparisons.

Applied Materials (AMAT): Strong business results, negative stock reaction

Applied Materials reported record quarterly revenue of $10.41 billion, an increase of 53% year over year.

Nevertheless, its shares declined approximately 2.74% in the first regular trading session following the announcement, closing Friday at $370.50 compared with $380.95 before the release.

There was also an interesting intraday recovery. Shares fell as low as $352.23 on Friday before recovering substantially by the close.

That suggests the initial selling did not retain its full advantage throughout the session, although the stock still finished lower.

What to watch: Whether AMAT can repair the negative earnings reaction or encounters further selling.

Its performance is relevant to semiconductor-sector sentiment, although its business exposure differs materially from Nvidia's.

Cisco Systems (CSCO): Even raised guidance did not prevent a selloff

Cisco provides another striking example of the difference between company performance and market expectations.

The company reported record quarterly revenue of $18.5 billion, up 24% year over year, and raised its fiscal 2027 revenue and earnings guidance.

Yet shares declined 6.24% on Friday, November 13, finishing at $95.64 versus the pre-earnings close of $102.01.

Because Cisco is a large company, its negative reaction also carried meaningful weight in the broader earnings assessment.

What to watch: Whether Cisco can reclaim part of its initial decline or whether sellers continue controlling the post-earnings repricing.

For Nvidia investors, Cisco offers a reminder that even strong reported growth and improved guidance do not automatically satisfy the market.

Nebius (NBIS): Selling continued beyond the first earnings session

AI infrastructure company Nebius experienced an even more severe negative response.

Shares declined approximately 16.84% on November 12, the day it announced quarterly results, and fell another 9.92% on November 13.

Across those two sessions, the cumulative decline relative to the November 11 close reached approximately 25.1%.

Unlike CoreWeave, which retained some of its initial gains, Nebius experienced continuing downside repricing.

What to watch: Whether selling begins stabilizing and a recovery develops, or whether the negative reaction continues.

A substantial decline can create potential opportunities, but it can also signal that investors are reassessing expectations. The size of the fall alone is not sufficient evidence that a stock has become attractive.

Nu Holdings (NU): Evidence that the market is not uniformly bearish

It would be a mistake to characterize the entire earnings environment as hostile.

Nu Holdings, the parent company of Nubank, provides an important counterexample.

The company reported record quarterly net income of approximately $1.1 billion, while its shares advanced 11.75% on November 13.

The move exceeded the approximately 7.27% options-implied earnings move identified in the earnings research.

This illustrates that investors are still prepared to reward selected companies aggressively.

What to watch: Whether Nu Holdings can preserve its substantial positive earnings reaction over the following trading sessions.

Its performance offers a useful contrast with the technology infrastructure names and reinforces the view that market behavior is selective rather than uniformly bearish.

What would improve the earnings mood from here?

For the current cautious assessment to become more constructive, investors would ideally want to see several developments.

First, positive post-earnings reactions should become more widespread. A healthier market would have a greater proportion of reporting companies advancing rather than depending on a relatively small group of winners.

Second, influential companies should contribute positively. Strong gains concentrated among smaller companies are less persuasive for overall market sentiment if large-cap earnings reactions remain negative.

Third, and perhaps most importantly, positive earnings moves should begin demonstrating better follow-through.

A company that rallies after results and retains most of those gains provides different information from one that rallies initially but then gives back nearly everything.

Conversely, further deterioration in the earnings environment would become more convincing if negative reactions continued broadening, large companies remained under pressure and initially positive reactions repeatedly failed.

There is also a middle ground: some stocks recover while others continue falling, leaving the broader environment selective and difficult to characterize as either strongly bullish or strongly bearish.

That is broadly where the latest assessment stands, with the balance of evidence modestly favoring caution.

The Nvidia earnings reaction may matter more than the headline numbers

Nvidia's upcoming announcement provides a particularly important opportunity to test investor appetite for AI-related stocks.

An encouraging result would not simply involve Nvidia delivering strong financial numbers.

More persuasive evidence of improving market confidence would involve investors rewarding the report and maintaining that positive reaction beyond the initial enthusiasm.

Conversely, an initially positive reaction that quickly fades would resemble the behavior already observed in CoreWeave, although the two companies have different financial characteristics and investor expectations.

A negative first reaction followed by a recovery would offer a different interpretation again, potentially demonstrating that initial selling pressure was not sustainable.

For this reason, Wednesday's regular trading session, November 18, could become especially informative.

The key question is not whether Nvidia can produce impressive earnings. It is whether the earnings are strong enough relative to expectations to persuade investors to keep buying.

The latest investingLive earnings-mood reading of 4/10 suggests caution is appropriate when interpreting the first reaction.

It does not predict Nvidia's direction.

Meanwhile, CoreWeave, Applied Materials, Cisco, Nebius and Nu Holdings provide a useful group of recent earnings reporters to monitor for signs that broader market confidence is improving, deteriorating or remaining highly selective.

In the current environment, traders may learn as much from what happens after the initial earnings reaction as from the reaction itself.

Market observations and historical stock prices are based on completed U.S. trading sessions through November 13, 2026. The earnings-mood assessment is interpretive, not a statistical forecast. Educational market analysis, not investment advice.

This article was written by Itai Levitan at investinglive.com.

Japan Japan’s economy contracted an annualised 0.1% in the third quarter, its first decline in four quarters and short of forecasts for 0.3% growth. item.title: AI: Daily quotas come to DeepSeek, a visible sign of China’s AI chip crunch
item.description:
For investors, the DeepSeek report is a live data point in the debate over AI computing power. It suggests demand at China’s leading AI lab is running ahead of the chips it can get. Paired with the US plans to curb remote access in Southeast Asia, that could support the case for China’s domestic chipmakers and AI infrastructure suppliers. It also raises questions over how fast Chinese platforms can grow their AI services. For Nvidia, ahead of Tuesday’s results, it underlines how much Chinese demand is still unmet, and how much of it depends on routes Washington may now close. Until DeepSeek confirms the changes, markets are likely to treat this as a signal rather than a catalyst.

---

China’s best-known AI lab is rationing its free chatbot for lack of computing power, a rare public glimpse of the chip squeeze that US export controls were designed to create.

Summary:

  • DeepSeek has restricted use of its app and web service, citing insufficient computing power, according to multiple user reports.
  • Long conversations inactive for over seven days are no longer supported, and single inputs are capped at about 40,000 characters.
  • Daily conversation quotas have been introduced. Users who hit the cap see a “server congestion” message.
  • DeepSeek had not previously published a daily cap for its free chat. In May it quietly limited the regenerate and edit functions.
  • The company has not issued a public statement.
  • The reports come as the US drafts rules to block Chinese remote access to Nvidia chips in Southeast Asia.

Chinese artificial intelligence developer DeepSeek has restricted use of its consumer app and web service, citing a shortage of computing power, according to multiple user reports carried by Chinese financial media on Monday. The company has not issued a public statement on the changes.

Users said they received notices that, because of insufficient computing power, long conversations left inactive for more than seven days are no longer supported. The maximum length of a single input has also reportedly been cut to about 40,000 characters, and daily conversation quotas have been introduced. Users who reach the cap are told the service is congested and their usage quota has been reached.

The daily limit marks a clear break from past practice. DeepSeek has not previously published a daily message cap for its free chat service. It has relied instead on slowdowns and busy messages when demand peaked, and it offers no paid tier that lets users skip the queue.

It is also not the first sign of strain. In late May, users found that DeepSeek had quietly capped how often they could regenerate or edit responses, a move widely read at the time as a response to tight computing capacity.

The reported limits matter beyond one app because they offer a rare, visible signal of how scarce advanced computing power may be for Chinese AI developers. US export controls bar China from buying Nvidia’s most advanced chips directly, and companies have relied on smuggling and remote access to data centers in Southeast Asia to fill the gap. That second route is now under threat. The Wall Street Journal has reported that the US Commerce Department is drafting rules to restrict chip exports to Malaysia, Indonesia and Singapore and to block Chinese remote access.

If those rules go ahead, pressure on Chinese developers’ computing budgets could intensify. That would strengthen the case for domestic chip suppliers, while making it harder for Chinese labs to keep up with fast-growing user demand.

For now, the details rest on user reports. Confirmation from DeepSeek, or an explanation of whether the limits are temporary, will show whether this is a short-term capacity squeeze or a lasting constraint.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: BOJ’s Takata calls for nimble hikes after 1.5% bid, says neutral rate may top estimates
item.description:
Takata’s speech is the clearest public argument yet for a faster BOJ hiking pace than markets assume. He rejects a fixed quarterly rhythm and argues for reaching the middle of the neutral range early, which puts a move beyond 1.5% within view. Because his views are his own and he has been outvoted, it doesn’t change December pricing by itself. But it supports the yen and adds upward pressure on front-end JGB yields, especially with USD/JPY near 160. His explicit link between real rate differentials and the currency also signals that BOJ hawks see rate hikes as a tool against yen weakness. On the same day as a weak GDP print, the debate on the board is now plainly about speed, not direction.

---

Takata wants the BOJ to stop hiking on a timetable and start hiking on the data, and with producer prices running at 7% and the yen near 160, he thinks the data already argues for moving faster.

Summary:

  • BOJ board member Hajime Takata said 2026 is a regime change, requiring nimble, data-dependent rate hikes rather than a fixed pace.
  • He laid out the case for his October proposal to raise the policy rate to 1.5% from 1.25%, and stressed that the views are his own.
  • He said underlying inflation has reached 2%, inflation expectations are above 2% and producer prices rose 7.1% in October.
  • He said Japan’s neutral rate could exceed market expectations, and the BOJ should move early towards the middle of the estimated 1.1% to 2.5% range.
  • He cited Japan’s world-lowest real policy rate and currency effects as reasons hikes are needed.
  • He said the cumulative effects of past hikes are still some way off, and AI investment should stay solid.

Bank of Japan board member Hajime Takata said in a speech to business leaders in Tokushima on Monday that the central bank should raise interest rates nimbly rather than at a fixed pace. He argued that 2026 marks a regime change for Japan’s monetary policy and that the neutral rate may prove higher than markets expect.

Takata was the lone dissenter at the October meeting, when he proposed lifting the policy rate to 1.5% from 1.25%. In the speech he laid out his reasoning in detail, stressing that the views were his own. He said the BOJ should not be bound by particular intervals or ranges anticipated in markets, and should instead respond to domestic price and economic conditions as well as developments overseas.

At the heart of his argument is a shift in the inflation picture. Takata said underlying inflation has reached the 2% target and medium- to long-term inflation expectations have risen above 2%, increasing the risk of second-round effects. He flagged producer price inflation of 7.1% in October and faster pass-through of costs to consumers, and said energy costs driven by the Middle East conflict could push prices above target. As a result, he argued, the BOJ should shift from encouraging inflation towards showing markets its determination to prevent prices overshooting, while taking account of the effects of the currency.

He also pointed to the yen. Japan’s real policy rate remains the lowest in the world. With some currency market participants focusing on real rate differentials, he said, price pressures transmitted through the exchange rate are one reason hikes are needed now.

On the neutral rate, Takata said Japan’s policy rate has only just reached the neutral zone, which the BOJ estimates broadly at 1.1% to 2.5%. With central banks abroad raising rates, he warned that Japan’s neutral rate could end up higher than markets assume. He said the BOJ should move early to a level near the middle of that range, which would give it room to hike or cut later.

Takata said the cumulative effects of past hikes are still some way off. He cited strong corporate balance sheets, accommodative financial conditions, a recovering global economy and AI-related demand, which he expects to remain solid despite turbulence in stock markets in early November.

His remarks come on the same day that data showed Japan’s economy contracted slightly in the third quarter, with markets watching whether the BOJ moves in December.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Goldman sees Brent at $78 by end-2027 as oil surplus returns, flags near-term upside risk
item.description:
Goldman’s path implies Brent averaging nearly $8 below current levels next year, and about $18 lower by end-2027. That gives oil bears a solid medium-term anchor. In the near term, though, the market is still driven by the war. Confirmation of the IRGC’s tanker-sinking claims could quickly rebuild the risk premium that Goldman expects to fade. Monday’s dip suggests traders are leaning toward the surplus story for now. The diesel forecast matters for inflation. At $150 a barrel, products stay costly even as crude eases, so energy keeps feeding into the inflation concerns Fed officials raised over the weekend.

---

Goldman’s message on oil is patience: a surplus is coming and prices should fall, but until the Gulf calms down, the risks over the next few weeks still point upward.

Summary:

  • Goldman Sachs forecasts Brent to average $88 a barrel in 2027 and ease to $78 by December 2027.
  • WTI is seen averaging $78 in 2027 and slipping to $70 by end-2027.
  • US wholesale diesel is forecast to average $150 a barrel in 2027, easing but still well above normal.
  • The base case assumes a 2 million barrel-per-day oil surplus in 2027.
  • Near-term risks are to the upside from shipping attacks, damage to infrastructure and a rebuilding risk premium.
  • Oil fell on Monday on surplus expectations, as Hormuz flows were reported near pre-war levels.

Goldman Sachs expects oil prices to drift lower over the next year as the market returns to surplus. It forecasts Brent crude to average $88 a barrel in 2027 and ease to $78 by December 2027, though it warned of upside risks in the near term from attacks on shipping in the Middle East, Reuters reported.

For US crude, the bank sees West Texas Intermediate averaging $78 a barrel next year and slipping to $70 by the end of 2027. Refined products should also ease but stay well above historical norms, with US wholesale diesel forecast to average $150 a barrel in 2027.

The core of the call is supply. In Goldman’s base case, oil production will exceed end-use demand by 2 million barrels per day in 2027. That surplus is large enough to pull prices down from current levels, even if some war-related risk premium lingers.

The bank was careful to present the risks as running in both directions. In the near term, it said prices could rise if attacks on shipping intensify, if oil infrastructure is damaged or if the risk premium rebuilds. Over the medium term, the risk is to the downside, through stronger supply, weaker demand or a smaller risk premium than it assumes.

That near-term risk is real. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards claimed over the weekend that two tankers struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz and that one of them, a supertanker carrying more than 2 million barrels, sank. There has been no independent confirmation.

Even so, prices fell on Monday on expectations of a supply surplus. Shipments through Hormuz were reported to be close to pre-war levels, and Washington eased domestic fuel movements by extending its Jones Act waiver. Brent was trading around $95.50 earlier in Asia, well above Goldman’s 2027 average, which implies significant downside if the bank’s surplus view plays out.

The gap between today’s prices and the forecast path leaves the oil market hinging on one question: whether supply disruption in the Gulf fades or flares up again. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Records show $12bn Nvidia chips to China, US drafts licence rules on Nvidia chip exports
item.description:
For Nvidia, the regulatory risk is now concrete just a day before results. Licence rules covering Malaysia, Indonesia and Singapore would put at risk a revenue stream that goes well beyond the officially reported China figures. Analysts will press management on how exposed the company is. The wider effects could hit data center developers and their backers in Southeast Asia, server makers that supply the region, and possibly memory chipmakers selling into AI build-outs. Construction plans in Malaysia could stall or move to other regions. For Chinese AI developers, losing remote access would make computing power scarcer, which could help domestic chipmakers in China over time.

---

Earlier:

  • Nvida stock analysis before its earnings
  • Jensen Huang weighs Nvidia comeback days after quitting over scandal, FT reports
  • Weekend: Bessent urges Nvidia to hire an outsider CEO, pouring cold water on a Huang comeback

---

The Huang scandal is turning into a policy reckoning: Washington looks set to close the Southeast Asian route that kept China supplied with Nvidia’s best chips, and the multibillion-dollar data center boom built on it.

Summary:

  • The US Commerce Department is drafting rules requiring licences for advanced chip exports to Malaysia, Indonesia and Singapore, barring Chinese remote access.
  • Records show Megaspeed arranged to send nearly $12 billion of top Nvidia chips to China between March 2024 and June 2025, though actual deliveries are unclear.
  • Malaysia has drawn more than $34 billion in data center investment and could become the second-largest hub in the world, largely on Chinese demand.
  • Malaysia says it is investigating Megaspeed and its local affiliate over possible re-exports.
  • Nvidia reported $12.4 billion in China revenue in the six months to late July, about 7% of its total.
  • Nvidia has already pushed cloud partners to cap Chinese clients at 30% to 49% of their business.

The US Commerce Department is drafting rules that would restrict exports of advanced AI chips to Malaysia, Indonesia and Singapore. The aim is to shut off a route that has let Chinese companies tap Nvidia’s most powerful processors through data centers in Southeast Asia, The Wall Street Journal (gated) reported, citing people familiar with the matter.

Under the proposals, companies shipping chips such as Nvidia’s Blackwell series to those countries would need a licence that bars Chinese customers from remotely accessing the computing power. The move would close a gap left open after the administration scrapped a Biden-era plan in May 2025 to cap chip imports in the region and did not replace it with other curbs.

That workaround has fuelled a construction boom. Malaysia has drawn more than $34 billion in data center investment, mostly from US and Chinese firms. Industry figures say it could become the world’s second-largest data center hub after Virginia, largely on the back of Chinese demand. Large Chinese technology groups are among the anchor tenants renting computing power there.

The issue has come to a head with the ouster of Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang over his affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed. Records seen by the newspaper show Megaspeed arranged to send nearly $12 billion of top-tier Nvidia chips to companies in China between March 2024 and June 2025. However, the records do not show how much was actually delivered or where it came from. Megaspeed said it operates lawfully, complies with export controls and has launched an internal investigation, and that Alice Huang left the company in August 2025. Nvidia says it works to prevent smuggling.

Malaysia said on Friday it will not allow itself to be used to get around export controls, and that it is investigating Megaspeed and its local affiliate.

The stakes for Nvidia are significant. item.title: China factory output slows to 4.8% in October, retail sales up just 0.4% as demand sags
item.description:
The data pushes in two directions for markets. Weak domestic demand and the investment slump support the case for more easing over time. But the view that no new stimulus will come this year limits any near-term “bad news is good news” rally in Chinese equities. The muted yuan reaction suggests the miss was largely expected. For commodities, slower factory output and the property slump are a headwind for iron ore and industrial metals. Softer Chinese activity also adds a mild drag on oil demand, against a supply backdrop still dominated by the Iran war. The Australian dollar is the most direct FX proxy for China, and could underperform if risk appetite weakens.

---

Earlier:

  • China’s October data shows the economy losing momentum on retail sales and industry output

---

China’s economy is running on one engine: AI exports are holding up growth while factories slow, shoppers retreat and property keeps sliding, and Beijing seems content to wait until that engine falters.

Summary:

  • Industrial output rose 4.8% y/y in October, against a 5.3% forecast and 5.5% in September.
  • Retail sales grew 0.4% y/y, below the 0.8% expected, despite a national holiday and the Singles Day shopping festival.
  • Fixed-asset investment fell 8.1% in January to October, worse than the expected 7.0% drop.
  • New home prices fell for a 41st month, though the annual decline eased to 2.4%, the slowest since November 2025.
  • Unemployment edged down to 5.1%.
  • Economists see the annual growth target as achievable and no new stimulus this year, with support for consumption possible in 2027.

China’s factory output slowed more than expected in October and consumer spending stayed weak, raising fresh questions about how long the world’s second-largest economy can lean on exports to carry growth, Reuters reported.

Industrial output rose 4.8% from a year earlier, official data showed on Monday, short of the 5.3% forecast and down from 5.5% in September. An official survey had already pointed to softer manufacturing sentiment in October, with new orders and new export orders weakening. That was despite trade data last week showing goods exports surging on demand for AI-related technology.

Retail sales grew just 0.4%, down from 1.1% in September and below the 0.8% expected. That is a weak result for a month that included a seven-day national holiday and the start of the Singles Day shopping festival. Growth in services spending also eased slightly, to 4.9% in the first ten months. A statistics bureau spokesperson acknowledged that households’ ability and willingness to spend need to improve.

The property slump remains the biggest drag. New home prices fell again in October, extending their run of monthly declines to 41 months, while resale prices posted a 42nd straight fall. The annual decline in new home prices did ease to 2.4% from 2.8%, the slowest since November 2025. Shanghai was the only major city to record rises in both new and resale prices. Property investment fell 21.6% in the first ten months, with new construction starts down 24.4%. Housing is the main store of household wealth, so falling values push families to save rather than spend. Economists say prices need to stabilise across cities, and excess inventory needs to clear, before the sector can recover.

Broader investment deteriorated further. Fixed-asset investment fell 8.1% in the first ten months, worse than the 7.0% decline expected and the steepest drop in this year’s run of contractions. The one positive was unemployment, which edged down to 5.1% from 5.2%.

Even so, economists do not expect a rush of new policy. With third-quarter growth at 4.5%, Beijing still looks on track for its annual target, and some analysts said they expect no new stimulus for the rest of the year. Others described 2026 as one of the weakest years for domestic demand in recent history. They said support for consumption could build in 2027, especially if exports start to cool and the drag from earlier trade-in subsidies fades.

For now, the AI export boom is carrying growth, and analysts say Beijing is likely to step up support for domestic demand only if that tailwind starts to fade. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Japan economy shrinks 0.1% in Q3, first fall in 4 quarters as inflation hits households
item.description:
The pushback from economists matters more for markets than the headline miss. If weak consumption is read as a sign of inflation rather than a reason to pause, December hike pricing should hold. That limits any lasting yen weakness from the data, although USD/JPY near 160 remains in intervention territory. The risk lies in the board split some economists flagged. Further soft consumption data could give the doves more influence and push hike timing back, which would weigh on the yen and lift JGBs. Oil is the link in the middle. Energy-driven inflation is both hurting households and pushing the BOJ to tighten, so higher crude makes the policy dilemma worse.

---

Earlier:

  • Japan Q3 GDP shrinks 0.1% annualised vs +0.3% expected as exports and consumers weigh

Recapping now.

---

Japan’s shoppers are buckling under inflation, but rather than giving the BOJ a reason to pause, the squeeze on households is being read as further proof that rates need to keep rising.

Summary:

  • Japan’s GDP fell an annualised 0.1% in Q3, against a forecast of +0.3% growth and an upwardly revised +1.7% in Q2. It was the first fall in four quarters.
  • Private consumption fell 0.3% as high prices, bad weather and fading tax-related demand weighed.
  • Net exports cut 0.6 percentage point as energy imports recovered.
  • Capex rose 1.6%, ahead of forecasts, helped by AI and labour-saving investment.
  • The economy minister expects a gradual recovery but flagged Middle East risks.
  • Economists see the BOJ’s tightening path intact, with a December hike possible, though some warned of a widening board split.

Japan’s economy unexpectedly contracted in the July to September quarter as rising living costs forced households to cut back on spending. Economists say the weakness is unlikely to knock the Bank of Japan off its tightening path, Reuters reported.

Gross domestic product fell an annualised 0.1%, against a median forecast of 0.3% growth, following an upwardly revised 1.7% expansion in the previous quarter. It was the first contraction in four quarters. On a quarterly basis, output slipped 0.02%, versus expectations of a 0.1% rise.

Households did most of the damage. Private consumption, which makes up more than half of economic output, fell 0.3%, slightly worse than the expected 0.2% drop. Persistent inflation, heavy rain and typhoons weighed on spending. Purchases of cars and air conditioners also fell back after a temporary boost from tax and regulatory changes in the prior quarter. Economists warned that higher prices linked to Middle East tensions will keep squeezing households’ purchasing power, even as wages rise.

Trade also took away from growth. Net external demand cut 0.6 percentage point, more than the expected 0.4 point drag. Imports jumped as oil and other energy purchases recovered after Japan diversified its supply following disruption from the war in the Middle East.

Business investment was the bright spot. It rose 1.6% against a 1.5% forecast, supported by spending on labour-saving technology and AI-related projects.

Economy Minister Minoru Kiuchi said better employment and income conditions, along with policy measures, should support a gradual recovery, but stressed the need to monitor the Middle East situation closely.

For the BOJ, which raised rates in June and September, economists say the miss changes little. Several argued that weak consumption is itself a symptom of high prices, which strengthens the case for further hikes, and many expect the next move as soon as December. One note cautioned, however, that if consumer weakness persists, it could widen divisions on the board and give more dovish members grounds to argue for caution.

That debate gets an early test later on Monday, when hawkish board member Hajime Takata speaks at 04:00 GMT (11:00 pm ET Sunday).

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Morgan Stanley goes max overweight global stocks, sees 15% S&P 500 upside on AI capex
item.description:
A maximum overweight call from a major house is a timely counterweight to the AI jitters around Nvidia and the QTS debt pullback. It could encourage dip-buying in tech and in the wider set of AI beneficiaries. The upgrades to Japan and Europe matter for flows. They support the Nikkei and Topix, already helped by a weak yen, and European stocks that have lagged the US AI trade. Morgan Stanley’s call for a slightly stronger dollar suggests the gains for non-US stocks are expected to come from earnings rather than currency moves. Gold bulls get some comfort from its backing for gold, but in the near term Fed pricing still dominates.

---

Where others see cracks in the AI trade, Morgan Stanley sees a buying opportunity: valuations have reset, the spending cycle is intact, and the next winners will be the companies putting AI to work.

Summary:

  • Morgan Stanley recommends a maximum overweight on global equities, saying the AI capex cycle remains intact.
  • It kept US equities overweight, upgraded Japan and Europe to overweight, and held emerging markets at neutral.
  • The bank raised its S&P 500 target, implying roughly 15% upside.
  • It expects a slightly stronger US dollar and favours investment-grade corporate bonds and gold.
  • Strategists said valuations have pulled back enough to justify a pro-risk stance.
  • They expect market leadership to spread beyond cloud vendors, with AI application revenue in focus by 2027.

Morgan Stanley has moved to its most bullish stance on global equities. It recommends a maximum overweight, on the view that the artificial intelligence investment cycle remains intact and will support economic growth and corporate earnings into next year, according to a report from Jinshi Data.

In a note dated November 15, the bank’s strategists kept US equities at overweight, upgraded Japanese and European stocks to overweight and left emerging markets at neutral. They also raised their S&P 500 target, implying roughly 15% upside from current levels.

The call rests partly on valuations. The strategists said the recent pullback in risk assets has made prices more attractive, prompting them to lean into risk rather than away from it. They also see market leadership broadening beyond the cloud computing giants that have driven much of the AI rally, and expect investors to focus more and more on revenue from companies deploying AI applications as 2027 approaches.

Across other asset classes, Morgan Stanley expects a slightly stronger US dollar and favours investment-grade corporate bonds and gold.

The timing gives the call added weight. It comes as investors weigh fresh questions over the AI trade. These include leadership turmoil at Nvidia ahead of its results on Tuesday, and signs of resistance in AI debt markets after Blackstone-backed data center operator QTS cut a planned private debt sale by about 60%. A Fed that is still raising rates is another headwind for valuations.

The gold view also stands out. Morgan Stanley’s preference for bullion contrasts with Goldman Sachs, which over the weekend trimmed its end-2027 gold forecast to $4,650 an ounce on expectations of further Fed hikes. Gold is trading near $3,876 in Asia.

For equity investors, the key question is whether AI spending keeps flowing through to earnings as financing costs rise. Morgan Stanley is betting that it will, and that the next leg of gains will come from the companies putting AI to work, not only from those building the infrastructure.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Oil price analysis: Sellers are losing momentum, but $86.75 remains the danger line
item.description:
WTI crude oil futures are trying to stabilize after breaking below a rising channel. Holding the $86.75-$87.25 zone could give buyers room to recover toward $92, while sustained weakness below it would keep $77-$79 in focus.

November 16, 2026 | Daily chart analysis | Prices in US dollars per barrel

Light crude oil futures still have a bearish daily-chart structure, but sellers are showing early signs of losing effectiveness. My key decision zone is $86.75-$87.25. Sustained trading below it would strengthen the case for another leg lower. Holding above it would give the developing stabilization a chance to become something more meaningful. Let's jump into my oil price analysis today, and as the week is starting:

At the analysis snapshot, WTI futures were around $88.09, above that zone but still below the broken rising channel and the daily 20-period exponential moving average near $92.16. The November 16 daily candle was still developing.

The analysis uses the continuous daily futures chart, with December 2026 shown as the front-month contract. These are futures reference levels, not interchangeable prices for Brent, spot crude or an oil ETF.

The channel broke. The rebound has not repaired the damage.

In my accompanying investingLive video, I explain the rising channel that framed crude oil’s recovery from the summer.

Its upper boundary connects the July 23 and September 15 highs. The lower boundary draws on the August 5-6 lows, with subsequent tests around October 6 and November 3.

Price then broke below that lower boundary. I interpret that as a bearish flag activation: the rising recovery structure gave way, increasing the risk of renewed downside.

The rebound that followed has not reached either the broken channel boundary or the daily 20 EMA, a moving average that gives more weight to recent prices. That limited recovery is a supplementary bearish sign.

Friday’s candle also did not provide the convincing upside follow-through I would want to see before giving buyers greater credit.

My broader lean therefore remains bearish, even though the latest evidence gives a reason to watch for stabilization. A slowing decline and a repaired trend are different stages of a possible recovery.

Why $86.75-$87.25 is my “zone in the sand”

Rather than treating one exact price as a switch, I am watching the full $86.75-$87.25 area.

Below $86.75: the downside scenario strengthens.

If crude sustains trading below the lower edge, my next broader area of interest is $77-$79. That is a conditional price objective, not a prediction that oil must reach it within a particular number of days.

“Sustains below” should match the trader’s timeframe. Some may look for two-hour candles holding below the level; others may require a daily close. A brief move through support followed by a recovery is different from price repeatedly holding beneath it.

Above $87.25: stabilization has room to develop.

If price can establish support above the zone, a recovery toward the daily 20 EMA near $92 becomes more plausible. That reference will move as new daily candles develop.

However, reaching the moving average would still leave another test overhead: the lower boundary of the broken channel. Bulls would need to at least challenge that boundary, with a sustained recovery back inside the channel providing stronger evidence that the breakdown is losing force.

Inside the zone: the outcome remains unresolved.

Repeated crossings would show that neither side has secured control. There is no need to turn every visit to this area into a trade.

Selling is becoming less effective, but buyers still need to prove themselves

The comparison between the last two trading weeks adds an important qualification to the bearish chart.

On Wednesday, November 4, crude fell $8.77 from its daily open to its close. On Wednesday, November 11, it finished almost unchanged from its open, although it again closed weakly within the day’s range.

Both weeks then produced Thursday-Friday recoveries. The November 12-13 rebound made slightly greater price progress on considerably lower traded volume.

That may indicate less resistance from sellers. However, a lower-volume rebound can also reflect limited buying participation, so it does not establish a durable reversal by itself.

Friday provided another potentially constructive clue. Crude finished slightly above its session open despite a selling imbalance in executed trades. Meanwhile, the price attracting the most traded volume shifted upward from $86.85 to $88.65.

In plain English, selling activity was not producing the downward progress that bears would normally want, while trading became concentrated at a higher price. That is consistent with buyers absorbing some selling pressure, although it does not identify who those buyers were or prove their intentions.

The useful distinction is that sellers may be losing control before buyers have established it. The latest evidence supports watching for a reversal; it does not yet confirm one.

Oil news adds tension to the technical picture

The fundamental backdrop also contains competing forces.

Over the weekend, Reuters reported Iranian claims of tanker mine strikes in the Strait of Hormuz. Those reports were not independently verified. Bahrain also said it intercepted Iranian attacks, while renewed Houthi activity added to concerns about regional infrastructure and shipping security. These developments could support crude if they translate into meaningful disruption to oil exports.

The counterweight is improving supply. In its November oil market report, published November 13, the International Energy Agency said global supply increased by 2.3 million barrels a day in October and forecast a return to surplus in the fourth quarter as Gulf exports recovered faster than demand. IEA

My interpretation is that traders need to distinguish threatening headlines from evidence that fewer barrels are actually reaching the market. Continued export recovery would support the supply-surplus argument. Confirmed disruption could challenge it.

Readers can follow further developments in investingLive’s oil coverage.

A bearish outlook does not automatically mean shorting here

The purpose of this analysis is to identify where the outlook strengthens or weakens. To see what I showed on the above daily chart - view the light crude oil analysis video at the top of this article.

In short, below $86.75, sustained weakness would keep $77-$79 in view. Stabilization above $87.25 would give buyers a chance to work toward $92, followed by a test of the broken channel.

At around $88, the downside condition has not been established simply because the broader chart looks bearish. Equally, the recent improvement in selling effectiveness is not sufficient reason to declare a bottom.

For now, I am watching whether the early stabilization survives its next test. The $86.75-$87.25 zone is where that distinction becomes especially useful.

Educational only. Trade at your own risk.

This article was written by Itai Levitan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Weekend - Bitcoin fell to four-month low near $62,000 as crypto liquidations top $2 billion
item.description:
The weekend flush has removed much of the leveraged long exposure that built up before the drop. That lowers the risk of another forced-selling cascade in the near term, but it does not bring in new buyers by itself. Sentiment is fragile. Several possible drivers are in play at once: ETF redemptions, rate-hike expectations and lingering exchange-security worries after the Binance hack. With that many headwinds, a recovery will need confirmation from flows rather than from price alone. Ether’s steeper loss keeps the ETH/BTC cross under pressure heading into the new week.

---

Leveraged bulls paid for the weekend’s slide to a four-month low, and the bounce means little until ETF outflows stop.

Summary:

  • Bitcoin hit about $62,000, its lowest since July, before recovering to $64,910 by late Sunday afternoon ET. It was down 14.2% on the week.
  • Over the same period ether fell 18.2% to $1,815 and Solana lost 19.7% to $71.68.
  • Crypto liquidations totalled $2.02 billion from 8 a.m. ET Saturday to 8 a.m. ET Sunday. Longs made up $1.68 billion and shorts $342.4 million. The live 24-hour tally had eased to $742.9 million by about 4:30 p.m. ET Sunday.
  • Changpeng Zhao said Binance had not sold crypto after its Oct. 29 hack and that he had personally bought crypto in recent days.
  • Zhao cited ETF outflows, Fed rate-hike expectations, investors possibly raising cash for Anthropic’s IPO, and security concerns as possible causes.
  • Spot bitcoin ETFs had $1.91 billion in net outflows over seven straight sessions through Friday. Spot ether ETFs shed $398.9 million last week, their seventh straight weekly outflow, one short of the record of eight.

Bitcoin dropped to its lowest level since July over the weekend, trading as low as $62,000 before recovering to $64,910 by late Sunday afternoon US time, according to The Block’s price data. That still left the world’s largest cryptocurrency down 14.2% over the past seven days, and the selloff spread across the market to trigger roughly $2 billion in forced position closures.

The damage was heavier further along the risk curve. Ether fell 18.2% over the week to $1,815, while Solana lost 19.7% to trade at $71.68, The Block reported. Ether underperforming bitcoin in a broad selloff is a familiar pattern, but a weaker ETH/BTC relationship on its own does not mean ether is cheap or due to catch up.

CoinGlass hourly data showed crypto liquidations totalled $2.02 billion between 8 a.m. ET Saturday and 8 a.m. ET Sunday. Long positions accounted for $1.68 billion of that, against $342.4 million in shorts. A liquidation happens when an exchange closes a leveraged trade because the trader’s margin can no longer cover losses, and those forced sales can push prices lower and trigger the next round of liquidations. The roughly five-to-one skew toward longs shows that traders were leaning bullish with borrowed money going into the drop. By about 4:30 p.m. ET Sunday, the live 24-hour tally on CoinGlass had eased to $742.9 million as prices steadied.

Binance co-founder and former CEO Changpeng Zhao used a post on X to deny rumours that the exchange had been selling crypto in the wake of its record hack on Oct. 29. Zhao said he had personally bought crypto over the past few days using stablecoins he recently received. He pointed to withdrawals from US spot bitcoin ETFs and expectations of another Federal Reserve rate hike as possible drivers of the slide, and suggested some investors may be raising cash for Anthropic’s planned IPO. He also cited lingering security concerns after the Binance hack. Those explanations are Zhao’s view rather than established causes.

The ETF data does support part of that argument. US spot bitcoin ETFs recorded $1.91 billion in net outflows across seven straight trading sessions through Friday, The Block reported earlier. Spot ether ETFs lost $398.9 million last week, their seventh consecutive week of withdrawals and one short of the record run of eight. Outflows show reduced demand through these products, but they do not by themselves tell us who is selling or why.

What to watch next: the first test is whether bitcoin can hold above the weekend low near $62,000 now that much of the leveraged long exposure has been cleared out. A halt to the ETF outflow streak, ideally confirmed over several completed sessions, would add evidence that product demand is stabilising. If spot ether ETFs post an eighth straight week of withdrawals, they would match their record. One calmer session after a liquidation flush is not proof of a bottom, so a practical approach is to watch both the flow trend and the price response before treating the recovery as durable. 

This little cartoon guy is hopeful!

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Gold slips toward $3,876 ahead of Warsh as Fed speakers line up behind tighter policy
item.description:
How the market reacts to Warsh will depend on tone more than detail. If he gives weight to AI as a future disinflationary force, traders could read it as a reason the Fed can stop after a few more hikes. That would offer relief to front-end Treasury yields and to gold. If he echoes Schmid’s view that AI demand responds to rates, it backs a longer tightening cycle and supports the US dollar. Gold remains the most exposed asset. With ETF selling risk now flagged and $4,000 broken, a hawkish lean could extend losses quickly. For equities, his comments on AI land the day before Nvidia’s results and will feed straight into how investors value the AI trade.

-- Warsh has staked part of his Fed leadership on the idea that AI can ease inflation, and on Monday he makes that case to a room of colleagues who have spent the past few days warning it is doing the opposite.

Summary:

  • Fed Chair Kevin Warsh gives opening remarks at the Fed’s Productivity and Jobs Task Force Conference at 17:00 GMT (12:00 pm ET) on Monday.
  • The San Francisco forum looks at whether AI will lower inflation, raise prices or displace workers.
  • Schmid, Collins and Jefferson all stressed persistent inflation in recent remarks, and Jefferson cited PCE at 3.6%.
  • Markets are fully priced for a quarter-point Fed hike on December 8-9, from the current 3.75% to 4.00% range.
  • Gold slipped to around $3,876 in Asia, extending a slide of almost 7% since last Tuesday after Goldman cut its forecast.
  • Fed minutes are due on Wednesday at 19:00 GMT.

Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh gives opening remarks at the Fed’s Productivity and Jobs Task Force Conference on Monday at 17:00 GMT (12:00 pm ET), hosted by the San Francisco Fed. The appearance follows a run of hawkish commentary from his colleagues over the past few days, and a December rate increase is widely expected.

The forum will bring together technology executives, economists and employers to examine whether artificial intelligence will lower inflation, push prices higher or displace workers. It is the first major public event for one of five task forces Warsh set up after taking office in May. He flagged it in October, when he described the surge in AI investment as one of the factors behind higher inflation. Warsh has argued that AI could eventually help firms produce more at lower cost and ease price pressure. Some colleagues see the AI boom adding to inflation today, with the productivity gains still unproven.

That debate has been front and centre in recent days. Kansas City Fed President Jeff Schmid said inflation is uncomfortably above target and heading the wrong way, and rejected the idea that AI-driven demand is beyond the reach of higher rates. Boston Fed President Susan Collins backed a steady, gradual pace of hikes, but said the eventual rate path may end up higher than she had expected. Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said the trajectory of inflation is the most important signal for policy, and warned that higher energy prices risk a broader rise, with PCE inflation at 3.6% in September.

The Fed raised rates to a 3.75% to 4.00% range in September and held in October. Markets are fully priced for a quarter-point increase on December 8-9, with a small chance of a larger move.

Gold has taken the brunt of that hawkish shift. The metal slipped in Asian trade to around $3,876 an ounce, extending a slide of almost 7% since last Tuesday, after Goldman Sachs cut its end-2027 forecast to $4,650 from $4,800 on expectations of a further hike in March 2027.

Opening remarks at a themed conference may carry little direct policy guidance, and Warsh said in October that he does not prejudge meetings. Any comment on AI’s effect on inflation, however, will be read for clues about December. Fed minutes follow on Wednesday at 19:00 GMT.

Goldman’s second downgrade and warnings of ETF selling point to the same problem for gold: a Fed that keeps hiking leaves little room for a quick recovery, even with central banks still buying.

Goldman Sachs has lowered its end-2027 gold price forecast to $4,650 an ounce from $4,800, its second downgrade in a month, as expectations of a longer run of Federal Reserve rate hikes cloud the outlook for investor demand, Investing.com reported.

The bank’s economists now expect the Fed to deliver a third quarter-point increase in March 2027, on top of the December hike that was already in Goldman’s base case. A rising policy rate is likely to weigh on private-sector investment in gold through early next year, even as central banks keep buying. In practice, the new target lines up with the bear-case scenario Goldman flagged in its previous note, which effectively moves that outcome into the main forecast.

Goldman’s first cut, earlier this month, lowered its end-2026 target to $4,150 from $4,650 and its end-2027 target to $4,800 from $5,400. The bank remains constructive over the longer run. It expects central banks to buy around 60 tonnes a month through 2026 and 2027. It still sees roughly 16% upside from current prices by December 2027, once the Fed starts cutting rates late next year and private demand returns.

The near-term picture is more fragile. Gold has fallen almost 7%, or about $290, since last Tuesday and is trading around $3,890. Analysts at a major European bank noted that rate expectations and bond yields have not risen enough over that time to fully explain the slide. They warned that exchange-traded fund investors could start selling into the weakness, which would push prices lower still. That is a risk rather than a confirmed wave of outflows, but it marks a shift from late October, when the same analysts described gold’s drop as excessive.

The common thread is the Fed. Hot inflation, and talk from some officials of a larger hike next month, have hardened the market’s hawkish bias. Higher oil prices tied to the Middle East conflict have fed that view rather than supporting gold as a haven.

Near-term tests include US retail sales and industrial production on Tuesday, and the minutes of the Fed’s latest meeting on November 18.

item.title: ICYMI: Fed’s Jefferson says inflation is the key signal for rates, with PCE still at 3.6%
item.description:
Jefferson’s comments support pricing for a December hike without adding to the half-point tail, which suits the steady, gradual camp. By naming energy as the main channel for broader inflation, he makes Fed expectations sensitive to oil. Any renewed jump in crude tied to the Iran war and Hormuz shipping risk would feed quickly into rate pricing and the US dollar. His upbeat view on growth and jobs also removes an easy reason to pause. That keeps front-end Treasury yields supported, and continues to put gold under pressure from the Fed’s tightening path.

---

With unemployment steady and growth near potential, Jefferson has made it plain that inflation, and energy-driven inflation in particular, now sets the Fed’s course.

Summary:

  • Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said the trajectory of inflation is the most important signal for setting monetary policy.
  • He said further moves should depend on data trends, the outlook and the balance of risks.
  • Headline PCE inflation was 3.6% in September and core PCE was 3.1%. October data so far shows pressures staying well above target.
  • He is concerned that higher energy prices could cause a broader, persistent rise in inflation, already visible in airfares and transport.
  • Unemployment was 4.1% in October, which he sees as consistent with maximum employment. Q3 GDP grew at an annualised 3.4%.
  • He voted with the majority to hold rates in October.

Federal Reserve Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said the path of inflation, rather than growth or jobs, will be the main guide for future interest rate decisions, as price pressures remain well above the central bank’s 2% target.

Speaking at the University of California, San Diego Economic Roundtable on Friday, Jefferson said further policy moves should be decided by carefully weighing trends in the data, the changing outlook and the balance of risks, ANI reported. He described inflation’s trajectory as the more important signal for setting the stance of policy.

Figures cited in his speech showed headline personal consumption expenditures inflation at 3.6% in September, with core PCE, which strips out food and energy, at 3.1%. Jefferson said the October inflation data received so far point to price pressures staying well above target.

He flagged energy as the main risk. Jefferson said he remains concerned that higher energy prices could lead to a broader and more persistent rise in inflation, noting that the effect is already visible in airfares and transport costs. Strong demand for new technologies is also lifting prices of some goods, including memory chips.

By contrast, his assessment of the real economy was steady. Jefferson said labour market conditions have stabilised, with unemployment at 4.1% in October, a level he regards as consistent with maximum employment and expects to hold in the near term. The economy has gained momentum this year, he said, with third-quarter GDP growing at an annualised 3.4%, roughly in line with its potential.

Jefferson said he voted with the majority to hold rates at the Federal Open Market Committee’s October meeting. Since then, he said, activity and the labour market have remained broadly solid, while inflation readings have continued to show persistent pressure.

As vice chair, Jefferson’s views carry weight with the committee’s centre. By putting inflation ahead of a stable labour market, his remarks fit the Fed’s tightening bias, with markets widely expecting a quarter-point rate increase at the December meeting. Upcoming core PCE data will be a key test of that view. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Weekend: Bessent urges Nvidia to hire an outsider CEO, pouring cold water on a Huang comeback

Just as Huang’s allies were building a comeback campaign, Washington weighed in: the Treasury Secretary wants an outsider in charge and answers on Nvidia’s China sales within 10 days.

Summary:

  • Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Nvidia needs a dramatic leadership shakeup and should look outside the company for its next CEO.
  • His remarks came as Jensen Huang was reported to be discussing a return, backed by Silicon Valley allies.
  • Bessent wants to know whether Nvidia ignored warning signs that shell companies, many in Singapore, were funnelling its AI chips to China.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Nvidia needs a “dramatic shakeup” in its leadership and should look outside the company for its next chief executive. His comments push directly against reports that ousted CEO Jensen Huang is weighing a comeback.

Speaking on Fox News’s Sunday Morning Futures, Bessent said the allegations surrounding the chipmaker suggest the board should hire from outside as it searches for a new leader. His comments came on the same day the Financial Times reported that Huang has been discussing a return, with Silicon Valley allies assembling a “war room” to build support. Nvidia and a Huang spokesperson declined to comment to the newspaper.

Bessent tried to shift the focus away from Huang’s personal conduct and toward legal and national security questions. He said he wants to know whether Nvidia knowingly ignored warning signs that shell companies, many based in Singapore, were channelling its advanced AI chips to China, and whether the company pushed such sales to lift revenue and earnings. He said the board and its outside counsel should provide answers within the next 10 days.

Huang stepped down on Thursday after revelations of an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International whom US officials suspect of spying for China. Bessent said he had long backed adding Megaspeed to a trade blacklist, but noted that the decision rested with the Commerce Department.

The Treasury chief also pushed back on calls in Congress for legislation to lock in chip export restrictions. He argued that existing rules are sufficient and simply need to be enforced. Lawmakers from both parties are backing a bill that could pass within weeks.

Bessent’s comments raise the stakes for Nvidia’s board ahead of quarterly results on Tuesday, which interim chief executive Colette Kress will present. Nvidia shares fell about 12.5% last week. Huang has agreed to testify before lawmakers behind closed doors. The board’s handling of both the succession and the compliance review will now be watched closely in Washington as well as on Wall Street.

item.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6771 – Reuters estimate
item.description:
The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Japan Q3 GDP shrinks 0.1% annualised vs +0.3% expected as exports and consumers weigh
item.description:
A flat quarter made weak mainly by trade is unlikely to derail BoJ tightening plans by itself. Strong capex and positive domestic demand are the parts policymakers watch most closely. The miss still gives the yen little help just as USD/JPY presses toward 160, and that raises the stakes for any comments from Japanese officials on the currency. JGB yields may ease slightly at the front end if traders trim December hike bets. The bigger driver for the session is Takata’s speech later today, where a hawkish response to the data would quickly restore conviction. For the Nikkei, softer growth and a weak yen are a familiar, broadly supportive mix for exporters.

---

---

Japan’s Q3 stall was a trade story more than a domestic one: exports and cautious shoppers dragged, but strong business investment leaves the BoJ’s December hike case largely intact.

Summary:

  • Japan’s preliminary Q3 GDP contracted an annualised 0.1%, against forecasts of +0.3% growth and following +1.4% in Q2.
  • Quarter on quarter, GDP was flat at 0.0%, versus a forecast of +0.1% and +0.4% previously.
  • External demand subtracted 0.6 percentage point (forecast -0.4), and exports fell 0.2% q/q.
  • Private consumption fell 0.3% q/q, against a forecast of a 0.2% decline.
  • Capex rose 1.6% q/q, beating the 1.5% forecast after a 0.9% drop in Q2. Domestic demand added 0.6 point.
  • The GDP deflator rose 2.4% y/y, below the 2.6% forecast and the previous 2.6%.

Japan’s economy stalled in the July to September quarter. Preliminary data showed real GDP contracted at an annualised 0.1%, short of the 0.3% growth economists had expected and a sharp slowdown from 1.4% in the second quarter. On a quarterly basis, output was flat, against a forecast of a 0.1% gain.

The miss came from two places. External demand subtracted 0.6 percentage point from growth, more than the 0.4 point drag expected, with exports slipping 0.2% from the previous quarter. Private consumption, which accounts for more than half of the economy, fell 0.3%, a slightly deeper drop than the 0.2% decline forecast.

Business investment was the bright spot. Capital expenditure jumped 1.6% from the prior quarter, just ahead of expectations of 1.5%, and reversed a 0.9% fall in the April to June period. Overall, domestic demand added 0.6 percentage point to growth, which shows the weakness was concentrated in trade rather than in the domestic economy as a whole.

Price pressure across the economy also came in a little softer. The GDP deflator, a broad measure of prices across the economy, rose 2.4% from a year earlier, below forecasts and the previous quarter’s 2.6%, though still comfortably above the Bank of Japan’s 2% target.

The figures land at a sensitive moment for the BoJ, which held its policy rate at 1.25% in October and is widely expected to raise it to 1.5% in December. A flat quarter driven by trade, alongside firm capital spending and positive domestic demand, gives policymakers grounds to look through the headline number. The softer consumption reading, however, will give more cautious board members something to point to.

Attention now turns to BoJ board member Hajime Takata, who speaks later on Monday at 04:00 GMT (11:00 pm ET Sunday). Takata has dissented at recent meetings in favour of faster tightening, and his read on the data will be watched for any shift in the December debate. A revised GDP estimate is due next month and could change the picture if the capex or consumption figures are updated. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
